Choosing a Machine Learning Framework in R: A Practical Comparison

R
Machine Learning
tidymodels
mlr3
caret
unifiedml
Published

April 6, 2026

R has multiple mature frameworks for machine learning, each with its own design philosophy: caret, tidymodels, mlr3, SuperLearner, h2o, and the newer unifiedml. Choosing between them can be genuinely confusing.

In this post, let’s solve the same problem with each one: predicting house prices on a held-out test set using 5-fold cross-validation. The side-by-side code makes it straightforward to compare the frameworks and pick the one that fits your workflow best.

The Common Problem

We’ll use the classic Boston Housing dataset (available through MASS) throughout. A ridge regression (glmnet) and a random forest will be our two models, since every framework supports both.

library(MASS)
library(dplyr)

data(Boston)

set.seed(42)
idx   <- sample(nrow(Boston), 0.8 * nrow(Boston))
train <- Boston[idx,  ]
test  <- Boston[-idx, ]

X_train <- as.matrix(train[, -14])
y_train <- train$medv
X_test  <- as.matrix(test[, -14])
y_test  <- test$medv

All models answer the same two questions:

  • What is the test RMSE for ridge regression and random forest?
  • What is the mean 5-fold CV RMSE for each?

1. unifiedml: Minimal Wrapper, Maximum Flexibility

unifiedml (v0.2.1, released April 2026) is the newest entry. It provides a single R6 class, Model, that wraps any R modeling function following standard conventions, with automatic task detection and built-in interpretability.

install.packages("unifiedml")
library(unifiedml)
library(glmnet)

# --- Ridge Regression ---
mod_ridge <- Model$new(glmnet::glmnet)
mod_ridge$fit(X_train, y_train, alpha = 0, lambda = 0.1)

preds_ridge <- mod_ridge$predict(X_test)
rmse_ridge  <- sqrt(mean((preds_ridge - y_test)^2))
cat("Ridge test RMSE:", round(rmse_ridge, 3), "\n")

# 5-fold CV
cv_ridge <- cross_val_score(mod_ridge, X_train, y_train, cv = 5L)
cat("Ridge mean CV RMSE:", round(mean(cv_ridge), 3), "\n")
library(randomForest)

# --- Random Forest ---
mod_rf <- Model$new(randomForest::randomForest)
mod_rf$fit(X_train, y_train, ntree = 500)

preds_rf <- mod_rf$predict(X_test)
rmse_rf  <- sqrt(mean((preds_rf - y_test)^2))
cat("RF test RMSE:", round(rmse_rf, 3), "\n")

# 5-fold CV
cv_rf <- cross_val_score(mod_rf, X_train, y_train, cv = 5L)
cat("RF mean CV RMSE:", round(mean(cv_rf), 3), "\n")
# Built-in feature importance via numerical derivatives
mod_rf$summary()

# Partial dependence plot (no extra packages needed)
mod_rf$plot(feature = "rm")

What stands out: The interface is identical for both models. Only Model$new(fn) changes. Auto-detects regression from the numeric y. The $summary() and $plot() interpretability tools work on any model without additional packages.

Note

unifiedml intentionally has no preprocessing or tuning built in. It’s designed for rapid prototyping and exploration, not production pipelines.

2. caret: The Battle-Tested Veteran

caret (Classification And REgression Training) was the first serious attempt at a unified ML interface in R, written by Max Kuhn in 2007. It wraps over 200 algorithms behind a single train() function and handles cross-validation and tuning in one call. It is now in soft-maintenance mode (Kuhn moved on to build tidymodels) but is still widely used in production systems.

install.packages("caret")
library(caret)

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5)

# --- Ridge Regression ---
fit_ridge <- train(
  medv ~ ., data = train,
  method    = "glmnet",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid  = expand.grid(alpha = 0, lambda = 0.1)
)

preds_ridge <- predict(fit_ridge, newdata = test)
rmse_ridge  <- sqrt(mean((preds_ridge - test$medv)^2))
cat("Ridge test RMSE:", round(rmse_ridge, 3), "\n")
cat("Ridge mean CV RMSE:", round(min(fit_ridge$results$RMSE), 3), "\n")
# --- Random Forest ---
fit_rf <- train(
  medv ~ ., data = train,
  method    = "rf",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid  = data.frame(mtry = 4),
  ntree     = 500
)

preds_rf <- predict(fit_rf, newdata = test)
rmse_rf  <- sqrt(mean((preds_rf - test$medv)^2))
cat("RF test RMSE:", round(rmse_rf, 3), "\n")
cat("RF mean CV RMSE:", round(min(fit_rf$results$RMSE), 3), "\n")
# Variable importance (model-specific)
varImp(fit_rf)

What stands out: Everything goes through train(). You specify the algorithm by a character string (method = "rf") from caret’s built-in registry. Preprocessing (preProcess) and tuning (tuneGrid) bolt on naturally. The downside: the algorithm registry means you must look up caret’s specific string name for each model.

Warning

caret is no longer actively developed for new features. New projects are better served by tidymodels (the official successor) or mlr3.

3. tidymodels: The Tidyverse-Native Ecosystem

tidymodels is a collection of packages (parsnip, recipes, rsample, tune, yardstick, workflows, and more) built by the same team as caret and deeply integrated with the tidyverse. It separates model specification, preprocessing, CV, and evaluation into distinct, composable steps.

install.packages("tidymodels")
library(tidymodels)

# Convert to tibble (tidyverse convention)
train_tbl <- as_tibble(train)
test_tbl  <- as_tibble(test)

# --- Resampling strategy ---
folds <- vfold_cv(train_tbl, v = 5)

# --- Preprocessing recipe ---
rec <- recipe(medv ~ ., data = train_tbl) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

# --- Ridge model specification ---
ridge_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 0) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

# --- Workflow: bundle recipe + model ---
ridge_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(rec) %>%
  add_model(ridge_spec)

# --- Fit + CV ---
ridge_res <- fit_resamples(ridge_wf, resamples = folds,
                           metrics = metric_set(rmse))
collect_metrics(ridge_res)  # Mean CV RMSE

# --- Final fit and test evaluation ---
ridge_fit   <- fit(ridge_wf, data = train_tbl)
ridge_preds <- predict(ridge_fit, new_data = test_tbl)
rmse_vec(truth = test_tbl$medv, estimate = ridge_preds$.pred)
library(ranger)

# --- Random Forest ---
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = 4) %>%
  set_engine("ranger") %>%
  set_mode("regression")

rf_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(recipe(medv ~ ., data = train_tbl)) %>%
  add_model(rf_spec)

rf_res <- fit_resamples(rf_wf, resamples = folds,
                        metrics = metric_set(rmse))
collect_metrics(rf_res)

rf_fit   <- fit(rf_wf, data = train_tbl)
rf_preds <- predict(rf_fit, new_data = test_tbl)
rmse_vec(truth = test_tbl$medv, estimate = rf_preds$.pred)
# Hyperparameter tuning (where tidymodels truly shines)
ridge_tune_spec <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 0) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet")

ridge_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(range = c(-3, 1)), levels = 20)

tuned <- tune_grid(
  workflow() %>% add_recipe(rec) %>% add_model(ridge_tune_spec),
  resamples = folds,
  grid      = ridge_grid,
  metrics   = metric_set(rmse)
)

show_best(tuned, metric = "rmse")
autoplot(tuned)

What stands out: The real power of tidymodels is composability. Swap set_engine("glmnet") for set_engine("ranger") and everything else stays unchanged: the recipe, the CV loop, and the metrics. The tune() placeholder makes hyperparameter search first-class. The tradeoff is the steeper ramp-up: you need to understand parsnip, recipes, workflows, rsample, and yardstick as distinct concepts.

4. mlr3: The Object-Oriented Powerhouse

mlr3 is the R6-based successor to the original mlr package, developed by a team at LMU Munich. It favors explicit object composition over function pipelines. Every concept (task, learner, resampling, measure) is a first-class R6 object you can inspect, modify, and combine.

install.packages(c("mlr3", "mlr3learners", "mlr3verse"))
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3learners)

# --- Define the task ---
task <- as_task_regr(train, target = "medv", id = "boston")
# --- Ridge Regression ---
learner_ridge <- lrn("regr.glmnet", alpha = 0, lambda = 0.1)

resampling <- rsmp("cv", folds = 5)
rr_ridge   <- resample(task, learner_ridge, resampling, store_models = TRUE)

# CV RMSE
rr_ridge$aggregate(msr("regr.rmse"))

# Test RMSE
learner_ridge$train(task)
pred_ridge <- learner_ridge$predict_newdata(test)
pred_ridge$score(msr("regr.rmse"))
# --- Random Forest ---
learner_rf <- lrn("regr.ranger", num.trees = 500, mtry = 4)

rr_rf <- resample(task, learner_rf, resampling, store_models = TRUE)
rr_rf$aggregate(msr("regr.rmse"))

learner_rf$train(task)
pred_rf <- learner_rf$predict_newdata(test)
pred_rf$score(msr("regr.rmse"))
# Benchmark multiple learners at once (a core mlr3 strength)
design <- benchmark_grid(
  tasks     = task,
  learners  = list(learner_ridge, learner_rf, lrn("regr.featureless")),
  resamplings = resampling
)

bmr     <- benchmark(design)
bmr$aggregate(msr("regr.rmse"))[, .(learner_id, regr.rmse)]
# Tuning with mlr3tuning
library(mlr3tuning)

learner_tune <- lrn("regr.glmnet",
                    alpha  = 0,
                    lambda = to_tune(1e-3, 10, logscale = TRUE))

at <- auto_tuner(
  tuner     = tnr("grid_search", resolution = 15),
  learner   = learner_tune,
  resampling = rsmp("cv", folds = 5),
  measure   = msr("regr.rmse")
)

at$train(task)
at$tuning_result

What stands out: mlr3 is the most explicit framework. The task type, the learner, the resampling, and the measure are all stated explicitly via string IDs. This verbosity is also a strength: you can inspect any object (learner$param_set, task$feature_names) and swap components without rewriting surrounding code. The benchmark() function makes multi-model comparison effortless.

Tip

The mlr3verse meta-package installs the full ecosystem: mlr3tuning, mlr3pipelines, mlr3viz, and more. It’s the fastest way to get started.

5. SuperLearner: When You Want an Optimal Ensemble

SuperLearner implements the super learner algorithm: it fits a library of base learners, then learns the optimal weighted combination using cross-validation.

install.packages("SuperLearner")
library(SuperLearner)
library(glmnet)
library(randomForest)

# SuperLearner expects named wrapper functions (SL.*)
fit_sl <- SuperLearner(
  Y         = y_train,
  X         = as.data.frame(X_train),
  SL.library = c("SL.glmnet", "SL.randomForest", "SL.mean"),
  family    = gaussian(),
  cvControl = list(V = 5)   # 5-fold internal CV
)

fit_sl          # Shows the learner weights
fit_sl$coef     # Optimal combination coefficients
preds_sl <- predict(fit_sl, newdata = as.data.frame(X_test))
rmse_sl  <- sqrt(mean((preds_sl$pred - y_test)^2))
cat("SuperLearner ensemble test RMSE:", round(rmse_sl, 3), "\n")
# Cross-validated SuperLearner: honest estimate of ensemble performance
cv_sl <- CV.SuperLearner(
  Y         = y_train,
  X         = as.data.frame(X_train),
  SL.library = c("SL.glmnet", "SL.randomForest"),
  family    = gaussian(),
  V         = 5
)

summary(cv_sl)
plot(cv_sl)

What stands out: SuperLearner’s key idea is that instead of picking one best algorithm, you let cross-validation figure out the optimal blend. In practice this nearly always matches or beats any single learner. The interface is deliberately simple, with most of the complexity hidden inside the ensemble logic. It’s particularly popular in biostatistics and causal inference, since it integrates directly with tmle and AIPW.

Note

SuperLearner has no built-in preprocessing or feature engineering. All transformations must happen before passing X to SuperLearner().

6. h2o: Scalable AutoML

h2o runs a local Java server and exposes parallelized implementations of GLM, GBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, Deep Learning, and fully automatic AutoML. It’s the right tool when data doesn’t fit comfortably in memory, or when you want a fully automated model search.

install.packages("h2o")  # Requires Java >= 8
library(h2o)
h2o.init(nthreads = -1, max_mem_size = "4g")   # Uses all available cores

train_h2o <- as.h2o(train)
test_h2o  <- as.h2o(test)

x_cols <- setdiff(names(train), "medv")
y_col  <- "medv"
# --- Ridge Regression ---
fit_ridge <- h2o.glm(
  x             = x_cols,
  y             = y_col,
  training_frame = train_h2o,
  alpha         = 0,
  lambda        = 0.1,
  nfolds        = 5,
  keep_cross_validation_predictions = TRUE
)

h2o.rmse(fit_ridge, xval = TRUE)   # 5-fold CV RMSE
h2o.rmse(h2o.performance(fit_ridge, newdata = test_h2o))  # Test RMSE
# --- Random Forest ---
fit_rf <- h2o.randomForest(
  x              = x_cols,
  y              = y_col,
  training_frame = train_h2o,
  ntrees         = 500,
  nfolds         = 5
)

h2o.rmse(fit_rf, xval = TRUE)
h2o.rmse(h2o.performance(fit_rf, newdata = test_h2o))
# --- AutoML: fully automated model search ---
aml <- h2o.automl(
  x              = x_cols,
  y              = y_col,
  training_frame = train_h2o,
  max_models     = 20,
  seed           = 42,
  nfolds         = 5
)

# Leaderboard: ranked by cross-validated RMSE
aml@leaderboard

# Best model
best <- aml@leader
h2o.rmse(h2o.performance(best, newdata = test_h2o))

# Explanation dashboard (SHAP, partial dependence, etc.)
h2o.explain(best, test_h2o)

What stands out: h2o.automl() requires essentially zero modeling decisions. It trains dozens of models, stacks the best ones, and returns a ranked leaderboard. The h2o.explain() dashboard gives SHAP values, partial dependence plots, and a full leaderboard in one call. The cost is setup complexity (Java dependency, h2o.init()) and that you’re locked into h2o’s own implementations rather than arbitrary R functions.

h2o.shutdown(prompt = FALSE)

Comparison at a Glance

unifiedml caret tidymodels mlr3 SuperLearner h2o
Models supported Any R fn 200+ (named) 100+ (engines) 100+ (IDs) Named wrappers Built-in set
Auto task detection ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌ ✅ (AutoML)
Preprocessing ❌ preProcess recipes mlr3pipelines ❌ Built-in
Hyperparameter tuning ❌ Grid/random tune_grid / Bayes mlr3tuning ❌ AutoML
Ensembling ❌ ❌ stacks mlr3stackr ✅ Core feature ✅ Stacked
Built-in interpretability ✅ Derivatives + PDP ❌ Via extensions Via extensions ❌ ✅ SHAP + PDP
Parallel CV Partial ✅ doParallel ✅ future ✅ future ✅ ✅ Distributed
Data format matrix / data.frame data.frame tibble data.table data.frame H2OFrame
Setup overhead None Low Low Low Low High (Java)
Learning curve Very low Medium Medium–High High Medium Medium
Active development ✅ 🟡 Maintenance ✅ ✅ 🟡 Stable ✅
Best for Quick prototyping Legacy code Production tidyverse Research / benchmarking Ensembles / causal Big data / AutoML

Lines of Code Comparison

Fitting ridge regression + 5-fold CV (same model, same data):

## unifiedml (4 lines)
mod <- Model$new(glmnet::glmnet)
mod$fit(X_train, y_train, alpha = 0, lambda = 0.1)
cv  <- cross_val_score(mod, X_train, y_train, cv = 5L)
mean(cv)

## caret (5 lines)
ctrl    <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 5)
fit     <- train(medv ~ ., data = train, method = "glmnet",
                 trControl = ctrl, tuneGrid = data.frame(alpha=0, lambda=0.1))
min(fit$results$RMSE)

## tidymodels (11 lines)
rec  <- recipe(medv ~ ., data = train_tbl) %>% step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
spec <- linear_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 0) %>% set_engine("glmnet") %>% set_mode("regression")
wf   <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(rec) %>% add_model(spec)
res  <- fit_resamples(wf, resamples = vfold_cv(train_tbl, v = 5), metrics = metric_set(rmse))
collect_metrics(res)

## mlr3 (6 lines)
task    <- as_task_regr(train, target = "medv")
learner <- lrn("regr.glmnet", alpha = 0, lambda = 0.1)
rr      <- resample(task, learner, rsmp("cv", folds = 5))
rr$aggregate(msr("regr.rmse"))

## SuperLearner (5 lines)
fit_sl <- SuperLearner(Y = y_train, X = as.data.frame(X_train),
                       SL.library = "SL.glmnet", family = gaussian())
predict(fit_sl, as.data.frame(X_test))

## h2o (7 lines, after h2o.init)
train_h2o <- as.h2o(train)
fit_h2o   <- h2o.glm(x = x_cols, y = "medv", training_frame = train_h2o,
                     alpha = 0, lambda = 0.1, nfolds = 5)
h2o.rmse(fit_h2o, xval = TRUE)

Decision Guide

The best framework depends on what you’re trying to do:

What do you need?
│
├─ Quickly benchmark 3–4 models with zero boilerplate?
│   └─ unifiedml ✓
│
├─ Feature engineering (imputation, encoding, scaling)?
│   ├─ You're in the tidyverse already → tidymodels (recipes)
│   └─ You prefer R6 / data.table → mlr3 (mlr3pipelines)
│
├─ Hyperparameter tuning?
│   ├─ Tidy workflow → tidymodels (tune_grid / tune_bayes)
│   └─ Research / reproducible benchmarks → mlr3 (mlr3tuning)
│
├─ Optimal ensemble without picking one model?
│   └─ SuperLearner ✓
│
├─ Data > 1 million rows / need distributed compute?
│   └─ h2o ✓
│
├─ Fully automated model search (AutoML)?
│   └─ h2o.automl() ✓
│
├─ Maintaining a codebase that already uses caret?
│   └─ Stay on caret. Migrating is low priority.
│
└─ Deploying models to production in R?
    └─ tidymodels + vetiver ✓

The Hybrid Workflow

These tools are not mutually exclusive. A practical workflow uses each for what it’s best at:

# Phase 1: Exploration with unifiedml
library(unifiedml)
for (fn in list(glmnet::glmnet, randomForest::randomForest, e1071::svm)) {
  mod <- Model$new(fn)
  mod$fit(X_train, y_train)
  cat(class(fn), "→ CV RMSE:",
      round(mean(cross_val_score(mod, X_train, y_train, cv = 5L,
                                 show_progress = FALSE)), 3), "\n")
}
mod$summary()          # Which features matter?
mod$plot(feature = "rm")  # Where does the relationship bend?

# Phase 2: Full CV + tuning in tidymodels
library(tidymodels)
rf_tune_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500, mtry = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("ranger") %>% set_mode("regression")

tuned <- tune_grid(
  workflow() %>% add_formula(medv ~ .) %>% add_model(rf_tune_spec),
  resamples = vfold_cv(as_tibble(train), v = 10),
  grid      = grid_regular(mtry(range = c(2, 13)), levels = 6),
  metrics   = metric_set(rmse)
)
show_best(tuned, metric = "rmse")

# Phase 3: Deploy with vetiver
library(vetiver)
final_fit <- last_fit(
  workflow() %>% add_formula(medv ~ .) %>%
    add_model(finalize_model(rf_tune_spec, select_best(tuned, "rmse"))),
  split = initial_split(as_tibble(Boston), prop = 0.8)
)
v <- vetiver_model(extract_workflow(final_fit), model_name = "boston_rf")
vetiver_write_plumber(v, "plumber.R")   # Ready to serve as a REST API

Summary

No single framework is universally best. The table below shows where each lives on the spectrum from fast and simple to powerful and complete:

Simple ◄─────────────────────────────────────────────────────► Powerful

  unifiedml    SuperLearner    caret    mlr3    tidymodels    h2o
      │               │           │       │          │         │
  prototype       ensemble     legacy  research   production  scale

If you’re new to ML in R, start with unifiedml to understand the problem, then graduate to tidymodels when you need preprocessing, tuning, or deployment. If you come from an academic background or care deeply about reproducible benchmarks, mlr3 is worth the steeper learning curve. And if your data is too big to fit in memory, h2o is hard to beat.

Happy modeling!
